deacon.e: From Middle English deken, dekne, from Old English diacon, from Ecclesiastical Latin diāconus, from Ancient Greek διᾱ́κονος (diā́konos, “servant, minister”).
deacon.g: A designated minister of charity in the early Church (see Acts 6:1-6).

dead.e: From Middle English ded, deed, from Old English dēad, from Proto-West Germanic *daud, from Proto-Germanic *daudaz.
dead.g: No longer living; deceased. (Also used as a noun.)

deadly.e: From Middle English dedly, dedlych, dedlich, from Old English dēadlīċ (adjective), from Proto-West Germanic *dauþalīk, from Proto-Germanic *dauþalīkaz (“deadly”, literally “deathly”). By surface analysis, dead + -ly. The adverb is from Middle English dedliche, from Old English dēadlīċe (adverb), from the adjective.

deaf.e: From Middle English def, deef, from Old English dēaf, from Proto-West Germanic *daub (“deaf”), from Proto-Germanic *daubaz (“deaf or stunned”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewbʰ- (“to whisk, smoke, darken, obscure”).

deafen.g: To make deaf, either temporarily or permanently.

deal.e: From Middle English del, dele, from Old English dǣl (“part, share, portion”), from Proto-West Germanic *daili, from Proto-Germanic *dailiz (“part, deal”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰ(h₁)-oy-lo- (“part, watershed”).
deal.g: A division, a portion, a share, a part, a piece.

deal.e: From Middle English delen, from Old English dǣlan (“to divide, part”), from Proto-West Germanic *dailijan, from Proto-Germanic *dailijaną (“to divide, part, deal”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰoh₁-i-l- (“part, watershed”).
deal.g: To distribute among a number of recipients, to give out as one’s portion or share.

dealer.e: From Middle English delare, from Old English dǣlere, from Proto-West Germanic. By surface analysis, deal + -er.
dealer.g: One who deals in goods, especially automobiles; a middleman.

dealing.e: From Middle English delynge, from Old English dǣling; equivalent to deal + -ing.

dear.e: From Middle English dere, from Old English dēore, dīere, dīore, dȳre (“of great value or excellence, expensive, beloved”), from Proto-West Germanic *diurī, from Proto-Germanic *diurijaz (“dear, precious; expensive”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *dʰegʷʰ- (“to burn; hot, warm”).
From Middle English dere (“fierce, severe, hard, deadly”), from Old English dēor, dȳr (“brave, bold; severe, dire, vehement”), from Proto-Germanic *deuzaz.

dearly.e: From Middle English derely, deorliche, from Old English dēorlīċe (“worthily, richly”), equivalent to dear + -ly.
dearly.g: In a dear or precious manner.

dearth.e: From Middle English derth, derthe, derþe, probably from Old English *dīerþ, *dīerþu, from Proto-West Germanic *diuriþu, from Proto-Germanic *diuriþō (“costliness, preciousness, honour”); corresponding to dear + -th (abstract nominal suffix).
dearth.g: A period or condition when food is rare and hence expensive; famine.

death.e: From Middle English deth, deeth, from Old English dēaþ, from Proto-West Germanic *dauþu, from Proto-Germanic *dauþuz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰówtus.
death.g: The cessation of life and all associated processes; the end of an organism's existence as an entity independent from its environment and its

deathly.e: From Middle English dethlich, from Old English dēaþlīċ, equivalent to death + -ly.
deathly.g: Appearing as though dead, or on the verge of death.

debar.g: To exclude or shut out; to bar.

debase.e: From de- + base, from Old French bas, from Latin bassus.
debase.g: To lower in character, quality, or value; to degrade.

debate.e: From Middle English debaten, from Old French debatre (“to fight, contend, debate, also literally to beat down”), from Romanic desbattere, from Latin dis- (“apart, in different directions”) + battuō (“to beat, to fence”).
debate.g: To participate in a debate; to dispute, argue, especially in a public arena.

debate.e: From Middle English debat, borrowed from Old French debat, deverbal of debatre, see Etymology 1 for more.
debate.g: An argument, or discussion, usually in an ordered or formal setting, often with more than two people, generally ending with a vote or other

debauchery.e: From debauch + -ery. First use appears c. 1642.
debauchery.g: An excessive indulgence in sensual pleasures; scandalous and immoral activities; involving sex, alcohol, or drugs without inhibition.

debt.e: From Middle English dette, dett, borrowed from Old French dete (French dette), from Medieval Latin dēbita, from Latin dēbitum (“what is owed, a debt, a duty”), neuter of dēbitus, perfect passive participle of dēbeō (“to owe”), contraction of *dehibeō (“I have from”), from de (“from”) + habeō (“to have”).
debt.g: An action, state of mind, or object one has an obligation to perform for another, adopt toward another, or give to another.

debtor.e: From Middle English dettour, from Old French detour, from Latin debitor, equivalent to debt + -or.
debtor.g: A person or firm that owes money; one in debt; one who owes a debt.

decay.e: From Middle English decaien (“to decrease, diminish”) and decai (“deterioration, decline in value”), from Anglo-Norman decaeir (“to fall away, decay, decline”), from Vulgar Latin *dēcadere, etymologically restored form of Latin dēcidere (“to fall down, to fail, sink or perish”), from de- (“of, from, away, down”) + cadere (“to fall”).
decay.g: Rot; any processes or result of organic matter being gradually decomposed, especially by microbial action.

decease.e: From Old French deces (Modern French décès), from Latin dēcessus (“departure”).

deceased.e: From decease + -ed, from Middle English deceas via Old French, from Latin dēcessus (“departure”), equivalent to dēced-, variation of dēcēdō, dēcēdere (“to go away”).

deceit.e: From Middle English deceyte, from Old French deceite, deçoite, from decevoir (“to deceive”), from Latin dēcipere (“to cheat, mislead”).
deceit.g: An act or practice intended to deceive; a trick.

deceive.e: From Middle English deceyven, from Anglo-Norman deceivre, from Latin dēcipiō (“to deceive; beguile; entrap”), from dē- (“from”) + capiō (“to seize”); see captive.

deceiver.e: From Middle English deceyvour, from Anglo-Norman decevour; by surface analysis, deceive + -er.
deceiver.g: A person who lies or deceives.

deception.e: From Middle English decepcioun, from Old French decepcion, from Latin dēcipiō (“to deceive”).
deception.g: An instance of actions and/or schemes fabricated to mislead someone into believing a lie or inaccuracy.

deceptive.e: From Middle French déceptif, from Latin dēceptīvus, from dēcipiō (“to deceive”).

decide.e: From Middle English deciden, from Old French decider, from Latin dēcīdere, infinitive of dēcīdō (“cut off, decide”), from dē (“down from”) + caedō (“cut”).
decide.g: To resolve (a contest, problem, dispute, etc.); to choose, determine, or settle.

decision.e: From Middle French, from Latin dēcīsiō, dēcīsiōnis, from dēcīdō (“to decide”).

deck.e: From Middle English dekke, borrowed from Middle Dutch dec (“roof, covering”), from Middle Dutch decken, from Old Dutch thecken, from Proto-West Germanic *þakkjan, from Proto-Germanic *þakjaną. Formed the same: German Decke (“covering, blanket”).
deck.g: Any raised flat surface that can be walked on: a balcony; a porch; a raised patio; a flat rooftop.

deck.e: From Middle English dekken, from Middle Dutch dekken (“to cover”), from Old Dutch thecken, from Proto-West Germanic *þakkjan, from Proto-Germanic *þakjaną (“to roof; cover”).
deck.g: To dress (someone) up, to clothe with more than ordinary elegance.

declaration.e: From Middle English declaration, declaracion, declaracioun, from Old French declaration (French déclaration), from Latin dēclārātiōnem, accusative of Latin dēclārātiō.
declaration.g: An emphatic or formal act of saying, telling or asserting something, by speech or writing; a decisive assertion or proclamation.

declare.e: From Middle English declaren, from Old French declarer, from Latin dēclārō (“to make clear”), from dē- + clārus (“clear”).

declaring.e: From Middle English declaring, declarynge, equivalent to declare + -ing (present participle ending).

decline.e: From Middle English declinen, and ultimately Latin declīnō (“to bend, turn aside, deflect, inflect, decline”, from dē- (“down”) + clīnō (“to bend, to incline”)), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱley- (English lean).

decorate.e: From Middle English decorat (“adorned”), from Latin decorātus, perfect passive participle of decorō (“to adorn, distinguish, honor”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from decus (“ornament, grace, dignity, honor”, decor- in compounds), akin to decor (“elegance, grace, beauty, ornament”), from decet (“adorn, befit”).

From Middle English decorat (“decorated, adorned”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more. Originally also used as the past participle of decorate; compare generate or communicate.

decorum.e: Borrowed from Latin decōrum, neuter form of decōrus (“proper, decent”).

decrease.e: From Middle English decresen, alteration of discresen, from Anglo-Norman, Old French descreistre (French: décroître), from Latin decrescere.
decrease.g: Of a quantity, to become smaller.

decree.e: From Middle English decre, decree, from Old French decré (French décret), from Latin dēcrētum.

dedicate.e: From Middle English dedicaten (“to dedicate”), from dedicat(e) (“dedicated”, also used as the past participle of dedicaten) + -en (verb-forming suffix), from Latin dēdicātus, the perfect passive participle of dēdicō (“to dedicate, proclaim”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).
dedicate.g: To set apart for a deity or for religious purposes; consecrate.

dedicate.e: from Middle English dedicat(e) (“dedicated”, also used as the past participle of dedicaten), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more. The nouns is derived through substantivization from Latin dēdicātus, see -ate (noun-forming suffix).

dedication.e: Originated 1350–1400 from Middle English dedicacioun, from Old French dedicacion (“consecration of a church or chapel”), from Latin dēdicātiō, equivalent to dēdicātus+-iōn.
dedication.g: The act of dedicating or the state of being dedicated.

deed.e: From Middle English dede, from Old English dēd, dǣd (“deed, act”), from Proto-West Germanic *dādi, from Proto-Germanic *dēdiz (“deed”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰéh₁tis (“deed, action”). Analyzable through Proto-Germanic as do + -th.
deed.g: An action or act; something that is done.

deem.e: From Middle English dēmen (“to judge; to criticize, condemn; to impose a penalty on, sentence; to direct, order; to believe, think, deem”), from Old English dēman (“to decide, decree, deem”), from Proto-West Germanic *dōmijan, from Proto-Germanic *dōmijaną (“to judge, think”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to set, put”).
deem.g: To hold in belief or estimation; to adjudge as a conclusion; to regard as being; to evaluate according to one's beliefs; to account.

deem.e: From Middle English deme, from the verb (see above).
deem.g: An opinion, a judgment, a surmise.

deep.e: From Middle English dep, deep, depe, from Old English dēop (“deep, profound; awful, mysterious; heinous; serious, solemn, earnest; extreme, great”), from Proto-West Germanic *deup, from Proto-Germanic *deupaz (“deep”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewbʰ- (“deep”).
deep.g: Extending, reaching or positioned far from a point of reference, especially downwards.

deeply.e: From Middle English deply, depely, from Old English dēoplīċe (“deeply”, adverb), from dēoplīc (“deep”), equivalent to deep + -ly.
deeply.g: To a deep extent or degree; very greatly.

deepness.e: From Middle English depnesse, from Old English dēopnes (“deepness; depth; an abyss”), from Proto-West Germanic *deupnassī, equivalent to deep + -ness.
deepness.g: The state or quality of being deep (either physically or metaphorically)

deer.e: From Middle English der, deer (“animal, deer”), from Old English dēor (“animal”), from Proto-West Germanic *deuʀ, from Proto-Germanic *deuzą, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewsóm (“living thing”), from *dʰéws (“breath”), full-grade derivative of *dʰwes-. Related also to Albanian dash (“ram”) (possibly), Lithuanian daũsos (“upper air.
deer.g: A ruminant mammal with hooves and often antlers, of the family Cervidae, or one of several similar animals from related families of the orde

defame.e: From Middle English defamen, from Anglo-Norman defamer (verb), defame (noun), and its source, Latin diffāmō, from fāma (“fame; rumour; reputation”).
defame.g: To disgrace; to bring into disrepute.

defeat.e: From Middle English defeten, from Middle English defet (“disfigured”, past participle) and defet (“defect”, noun), see Etymology 2 below.
defeat.g: To overcome in battle or contest.

defeat.e: From Middle English defet, from French deffet, desfait, past participle of the verb desfaire (compare modern French défaire), from des- + faire.
defeat.g: The act or instance of being defeated, of being overcome or vanquished; a loss.

defect.e: Borrowed from Latin defectus (“a failure, lack”), from deficere (“to fail, lack, literally 'undo'”), from past participle defectus, from de- (“of, from”) + facere (“to do”).

defective.e: From Middle English defectif, defective, from Old French defectif, from Late Latin dēfectīvus.

defence.e: From Middle English defens, defense, from Old French defens, defense, from Late Latin dēfēnsa (“protection”).
defence.g: The action of defending, of protecting from attack, danger or injury.

defence.e: From Middle English defencen, defensen, from Old French defenser or its etymon, Latin dēfēnsō.
defence.g: To furnish with defences; to fortify.

defend.e: From Middle English defenden, from Old French defendre, deffendre (Modern French défendre), from Latin dēfendō (“to ward off”), from Proto-Italic *fendō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰen-.
defend.g: To ward off attacks against; to fight to protect; to guard.

defender.e: From Middle English defender, deffender, defendere, defendour, defendoure, partly from Anglo-Norman defendour, from Old French defendëor; partly from Middle English defenden + -ere, equivalent to defend + -er.
defender.g: Someone who defends people or property.

defense.e: From Middle English defens, defense, from Old French defens, defense, from Late Latin dēfēnsa (“protection”).
defense.g: The action of defending or protecting from attack, danger, or injury.

defense.e: From Middle English defencen, defensen, from Old French defenser or its etymon, Latin dēfēnsō.
defense.g: To furnish with defenses; to defend, protect.

defer.e: Originally a variant of (and hence a doublet of) differ; from Middle English differren (“to postpone”), from Old French differer, from Latin differō.
From late Middle English differren (“to refer for judgement”), from Middle French déférer, from Latin dēferō.
defer.g: To submit to the opinion or desire of others in respect to their judgment or authority.

defiant.e: Borrowed from French défiant, from the verb défier. By surface analysis, def(i) + -ant.

deficient.e: From Latin deficiens, present participle of deficere (“to lack, fail, be wanting”); see defect.
deficient.g: Lacking something essential; often construed with in.

deficit.e: From French déficit, from Latin dēficit.
deficit.g: Deficiency in amount or quality; a falling short; lack.

defile.e: From Late Middle English defilen (“to make dirty, befoul; rape; abuse; destroy; injure; oppress”), a variant of defoulen (“to make dirty, defile, pollute; have sexual intercourse with; rape; etc.”) (compare also defoilen).
defile.g: To make (someone or something) physically dirty or unclean; to befoul, to soil.

defile.e: PIE word dwís The verb is borrowed from French défiler (“to march; to parade”), from dé- (prefix indicating actions are done more strongly or vigorously) + one or both of the following: filer (“to thread through (a crowd)”) (from Late Latin filāre, from Latin fīlum (“fibre, filament, string, thread”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰiH-(s-)lo-).
defile.g: To march in a single file or line; to file.

define.e: From Middle English definen, from Old French definer, variant of definir, from Latin dēfīniō (“limit, settle, define”), from dē + fīniō (“set a limit, bound, end”).
define.g: To determine with precision; to mark out with distinctness; to ascertain or exhibit clearly.

definite.e: From Latin dēfīnītus, past participle of dēfīniō, whence also English define.

deform.e: From Middle English deforme (“out of shape, deformed”), from Middle French deforme (modern French difforme (“misshapen, deformed”)), or directly from its etymon Latin dēfōrmis (“departing physically from the correct shape, deformed, malformed, misshapen, ugly.
deform.g: Having an unusual and unattractive shape; deformed, misshapen; hence, hideous, ugly.

deform.e: From Middle English deformen (“to disfigure, distort, or mar; (figuratively) to disfigure morally; to defame; to dishonour”), equivalent to de- + form, from Old French deformer (modern French déformer (“to contort, distort, twist out of shape.
deform.g: To change the form of (something), usually thus making it disordered or irregular; to give (something) an abnormal or unusual shape.

defraud.e: From Middle English defrauden, from Old French defrauder, from de- + frauder.
defraud.g: To obtain money or property from (a person) by fraud; to swindle.

defy.e: From Old French desfier, from Vulgar Latin *disfidare (“renounce one's faith”), from Latin dis- (“away”) + fidus (“faithful”). Meaning shifted in the 14th century from "be disloyal" to "challenge". Contrast confide, fidelity, faith.
defy.g: To challenge (someone) or brave (a hazard or opposition).

degenerate.g: Having deteriorated, degraded or fallen from normal, coherent, balanced and desirable to undesirable and typically abnormal.

degenerate.e: From a substantivation of the above adjective, see -ate (noun-forming suffix) for more.
degenerate.g: One who is degenerate, who has fallen from previous stature; an immoral or corrupt person.

degraded.g: Feeling or having undergone degradation; deprived of dignity or self-respect.

degree.e: From Middle English degre, borrowed from Old French degré (French: degré), itself from Latin gradus, with the prefix de-.
degree.g: A completed curriculum of study in tertiary education.

deject.e: From Old French dejeter, from Latin dēiectus, past participle of dēicere (“to throw down”), from dē- (“from, down from”) + iacere (“to throw”).

delay.e: From Middle English delaien, borrowed from Anglo-Norman delaier, Old French deslaier, from des- + Old French laier (“to leave”), a conflation of Old Frankish *lattjan ("to delay, hinder"; from Proto-Germanic *latjaną (“to delay, hinder, stall”), from Proto-Indo-European *leh₁d- (“to leave, leave behind”)), and Old Frankish *laibijan ("to leave".
delay.g: A period of time before an event occurs; the act of delaying; procrastination; lingering inactivity.

delay.e: From Middle English delaien, from Old French delaiier, a variant of delaissier.

delectable.e: From Middle English delectable, from Middle French délectable, from Old French delectable, from Medieval Latin delectare (“to delight”). By surface analysis, delect + -able. Piecewise doublet of delightable.
delectable.g: Highly pleasing; delightful, especially to any of the senses; delicious.

delegate.e: From Middle English delegat, from Old French delegat, from Latin dēlēgātus substantivized from the nominative masculine singular of dēlēgātus, the perfect passive participle of dēlēgō (“to send, assign, delegate”), see -ate (noun-forming suffix).
delegate.g: A person authorized to act as representative for another; a deputy.

delegate.e: From Middle English delegat(e) (“delegated”, used as a past participle and adjective), used as the past participle of delegate up until Early Modern English, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more.

delegation.e: Borrowed from Latin dēlēgātiō, dēlēgātiōnis, from dēlēgō: compare French délégation.

deliberate.e: From Middle English deliberat(e), borrowed from Latin dēlīberātus, perfect passive participle of dēlīberō (“to consider, weigh well”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dē- + *līberō / lībrō (“to weigh”)), from *libera / libra (“a balance”); see librate.

delicacy.e: From Middle English delicacie, from Middle English delicat, from Latin delicatus. Equivalent to delic(ate) + -acy.

delicate.e: From Middle English delicat, from Latin dēlicātus (“giving pleasure, delightful, soft, luxurious, delicate, (in Medieval Latin also) fine, slender”), from dēlicia + -ātus (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), usually in plural dēliciae (“pleasure, delight, luxury”), from dēliciō (“to allure, entice”), from dē- (“away”) + laciō (“to lure, to deceive”).
delicate.g: Easily damaged or requiring careful handling.

delight.e: Related with delectation, delicate, delicious and dilettante. The modern unetymological spelling (instead of expected delite) is influenced by light and other words ending in -ight, such as might, bright, etc. The -gh- may also be an attempt to represent the Latin -c-; compare obsolete indight for indict.

delightful.e: From Middle English deliteful, delitfull, equivalent to delight + -ful.
delightful.g: Pleasant; pleasing, bringing enjoyment, satisfaction, or pleasure.

delightsome.g: Characterised or marked by delight or delightfulness; very pleasing; delightful.

deliver.e: From Middle English deliveren, from Anglo-Norman and Old French delivrer, from Latin dē + līberō (“to set free”).
deliver.g: To set free from restraint or danger.

deliverance.e: From Old French deliverance (French délivrance), equivalent to deliver + -ance.
deliverance.g: The act of setting free or extricating from danger, imprisonment, bondage, evil, etc.

delivery.e: From Middle English deliveri et al., from Anglo-Norman, from Old French delivrer.

delude.e: From Middle English deluden, borrowed from Latin dēlūdō (“mock, deceive”), from de + lūdō (“to make sport of, to mock”).
delude.g: To deceive into believing something which is false; to lead into error; to dupe.

delusion.e: Borrowed from Latin dēlūsiō. (This etymology is missing or incomplete. Please add to it, or discuss it at the Etymology scriptorium. Particularly: “a direct borrowing from latin or e.g. through french?”)
delusion.g: An adamant belief in a falsehood despite incontestable evidence.

demand.e: From late Middle English demaunden, from Old French demander, from Latin dēmandō, dēmandāre.
demand.g: The desire to purchase goods and services.

demeanor.e: From Middle English demenure, from the verb Middle English demenen, demeinen (“to handle, manage”), from Old French demener (“to guide, conduct”), from de- + mener (“to conduct, lead”), from Latin *mināre (“to drive”) and minor (“to project or jut forth”).
demeanor.g: The social, non-verbal behaviors (such as body language and facial expressions) that are characteristic of a person.

demise.e: From Middle English demyse, dimise, dimisse, dymyse, from Middle French démise, the feminine singular past participle of démettre (“to put down, relinquish”); from Latin dēmissa, feminine singular of perfect passive participle of dēmittō.
demise.g: The conveyance or transfer of an estate, either in fee for life or for years, most commonly the latter.

demon.e: From Middle English demon, a borrowing from Medieval Latin dēmōn, daemōn (“lar, familiar spirit, guardian spirit”), from Ancient Greek δαίμων (daímōn, “dispenser, god, protective spirit”).

demon.g: Acronym of distinct electron motion particle: a quasiparticle, a type of massless neutral electron excitation associated with superconductiv

demonic.e: From Latin daemonicus, from Ancient Greek δαιμονικός (daimonikós, “possessed by a demon, sent by a demon”), from δαίμων (daímōn), equivalent to demon + -ic.
demonic.g: Pertaining to demons or evil spirits; demoniac.

demonstrate.e: Borrowed from Latin dēmonstrātus, the perfect passive participle of dēmonstrō (“to show, point at”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

demonstration.e: From Middle English demonstracioun, from Old French demonstration, from Latin dēmōnstrātiōnem, from dēmōnstrāre (“show or explain”), from dē- (“of or concerning”) + mōnstrāre (“show”). Morphologically demonstrate + -ion.
demonstration.g: The act of demonstrating; showing or explaining something.

demote.e: From de- (“down”) + promote (“advance in rank/status (ending abstracted)”).
demote.g: To lower the rank or status of.

den.e: From Middle English den, from Old English denn (“den, lair (of a beast), cave; a swine-pasture, a woodland pasture for swine”), from Proto-West Germanic *dani (“threshing-floor, barn-floor”).
den.g: A small cavern or hollow place in the side of a hill, or among rocks; especially, a cave used by a wild animal for shelter or concealment.

den.e: From Old French denier, from Latin denarius.
den.g: Abbreviation of denier (a unit of weight).

denarius.g: A small silver coin issued both during the Roman Republic and during the Roman Empire, equal to 10 asses or 4 sesterces. Roughly one day’s w

denounce.e: From Old French denuncier, from Latin dēnūntiō (“to announce, to denounce, to threaten”), from de + nūntiō (“to announce, to report, to denounce”), from nūntius (“messenger, message”).
denounce.g: To make known in a formal manner; to proclaim; to announce; to declare.

dens.g: A toothlike process projecting from the anterior end of the centrum of the axis vertebra on which the atlas vertebra rotates.

dense.e: From Middle French dense, from Latin dēnsus, from Proto-Indo-European *dens- (“thick, dense”) (whence also Ancient Greek δασύς (dasús)).

deny.e: From Middle English denyen, from Old French denoier (“to deny, to repudiate”) (French dénier), from Latin denegare (“to deny, to refuse”), from de- (“away”) and negare (“to refuse”), the latter ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *né (“no, not”).

depart.e: From Old French departir, from Late Latin departiō (“to divide”), from dē- (“away from”) + partiō (“part, divide”).

departure.e: From Old French deporteure (“departure; figuratively, death”). By surface analysis, depart + -ure.
departure.g: The act of departing or something that has departed.

depend.e: From Middle English dependen, from Old French dependre, from Latin dependeō, from dē- + pendeō (“to be suspended, hang”). In this sense, displaced native Old English hangian (“to hang or depend”).
depend.g: To be contingent or conditioned; to have something as a necessary condition

dependent.e: From Middle English dependaunt, dependent, from Middle French dependant (present participle of dependre (“to depend”)) and Latin dēpendēns (present participle of dēpendeō (“to depend”)). By surface analysis, depend + -ent.

deplete.e: Borrowed from Latin dēplētus (“empty”), from depleō.
deplete.g: To reduce the amount of; to remove (a substance from something)

deploy.e: Borrowed from French déployer (“to unroll, unfold”), from Old French desploiier, itself from des- + ploiier, or possibly from Late Latin displicāre (“to unfold, display”), from Latin dis- (“apart”) + plicare (“to fold”).
deploy.g: To prepare and arrange (originally military unit or units, i.e., to array troops) for use.

deport.e: Borrowed from French déporter. With the meaning of "behave", from Old French deporter (“behave”), from Latin deportō, from de- + portō.

depose.e: Recorded since c.1300, from Middle English, from Old French deposer, from de- (“down”) + poser (“to put, place”). Deposition (1494 in the legal sense) belongs to deposit, but that related word and depose became thoroughly confused.
depose.g: To put down; to lay down; to deposit; to lay aside; to put away.

deposit.e: Borrowed from Latin depositus, past participle of depono (“put down”).
deposit.g: Sediment or rock that is not native to its present location or is different from the surrounding material. Sometimes refers to ore or gems.

deprave.e: From Middle English depraven, from Old French depraver, from Latin dēprāvāre (“pervert, distort, corrupt”), from de- + pravus (“crooked, distorted, perverse, wicked”).
deprave.g: To speak ill of; to depreciate; to malign; to revile

depress.e: From Middle English depressen, from Old French depresser, from Latin dēpressus, perfect participle of dēprimō (“to press down, to weigh down”), from dē- (“off, away, down, out”) + premō (“to press”).

depression.e: From Middle English depression, depressioun, from Old French depression, from Latin dēpressiō. Equivalent to depress + -ion.
depression.g: A state of mind producing serious, long-term lowering of enjoyment of life or inability to visualize a happy future; any of several mental d

deprive.e: From Middle English depryven, from Old French depriver, from Medieval Latin dēprīvō, from Latin dē- + prīvō.
deprive.g: Used with “of”, to take something away from (someone) and keep it away; to deny someone something.

depth.e: From Middle English depthe, from Old English *dīepþ (“depth”), from Proto-Germanic *diupiþō (“depth”), equivalent to deep + -th (abstract nominal suffix).
depth.g: the vertical distance below a surface; the degree to which something is deep

depute.e: From French députer, from Latin deputo.
depute.g: To assign (someone or something) to or for something.

deputy.e: From French député, from Late Latin dēputātus (“appointed”).
deputy.g: One appointed as the substitute of others, and empowered to act for them, in their name or their behalf; a substitute in office.

deride.e: Borrowed from Latin dērīdēre, the present active infinitive of dērīdeō (“to laugh at, make fun of, mock, deride”), from dē- (prefix denoting putting down or subjecting to indignity) + rīdeō (“to laugh; to laugh at, mock, ridicule”) (further etymology uncertain, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *wert- (“to rotate.
deride.g: To laugh at or mock (someone or something) harshly; to ridicule, to scorn.

derision.e: From Old French derision, from Latin dērīsiōnem, accusative of dērīsiō, from dērīdēre ("to mock, to laugh at, to deride").

derive.e: From Middle English deriven, from Old French deriver, from Latin dērīvō (“to lead, turn, or draw off (a liquid), draw off, derive”), from dē (“away”) + rīvus (“a stream”); see rival. Unrelated to arrive.
derive.g: To obtain or receive (something) from something else.

descendant.e: From Middle English dessendaunte, borrowed from Middle French, from Latin dēscendēns, present participle of descendere, from dē + scandere (“to climb, ascend”).

descent.e: From Middle English and Anglo-Norman descente, from Anglo-Norman descendre (“to descend”); see descend.
descent.g: An instance of descending; act of coming down.

describe.e: From Middle English descriven, from Old French descrivre, from Latin dēscrībō (“to copy off, transcribe, sketch off, describe in painting or writing”), from dē (“off”) + scrībō (“write”); see scribe and shrive.

description.e: From Middle English descripcioun, from Old French description and its etymon, Latin dēscrīptiō, noun of action of dēscrībō (“to describe”). Equivalent to describe + -tion.
description.g: A sketch or account of anything in words; a portraiture or representation in language; an enumeration of the essential qualities of a thing

descry.e: From Middle English descrien, descriven in the 14th century already had the dual sense of "to proclaim, announce, make known" and "to see, discern, discover". On the one hand, the Middle English word is a loan Old French descrier (“to proclaim, announce, cry”), from des- + crier (“shout, cry”).
descry.g: To announce a discovery: to disclose; to reveal.

desecrate.g: To profane or violate the sacredness or sanctity of something.

desert.e: From Middle English desert (“wilderness”), from Old French desert, from Latin dēsertum, past participle of dēserō (“to abandon”). Generally displaced native Old English wēsten. False cognate of Egyptian dšrt.
desert.g: A barren area of land or desolate terrain, especially one with little water or vegetation; a wasteland.

desert.e: Borrowed from French déserter, from Late Latin dēsertō, from Latin dēsertus, from dēserō (“abandon”).
desert.g: To leave (anything that depends on one's presence to survive, exist, or succeed), especially when contrary to a promise or obligation; to ab

deserter.e: Borrowed from Latin desertor (“deserter”), from desero (“to forsake, to abandon”); or from desert + -er.
deserter.g: A person who has physically removed him- or herself from the control or direction of a military or naval unit with the intention of permanen

deserve.e: From Middle English deserven, from Old French deservir, from Latin dēserviō, from dē- + serviō.
deserve.g: To be entitled to, as a result of past actions; to be worthy to have.

design.e: From Middle English designen, from Old French designer, from Latin designō (“to mark out, point out, describe, design, contrive”), from de- (or dis-) + signō (“to mark”), from signum (“mark”).
design.g: A specification of an object or process, referring to requirements to be satisfied and thus conditions to be met for them to solve a problem

designate.e: Borrowed from Latin dēsignātus, perfect passive participle of designō, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix).

desirable.e: From Old French desirable. Morphologically desire + -able.
desirable.g: Worthy to be desired; pleasing; agreeable.

desire.e: From Middle English desir, desire (noun) and desiren (verb), from Old French desirer, desirrer, from Latin dēsīderō (“to long for, desire, feel the want of, miss, regret”), apparently from de- + sidus (in the phrase de sidere, "from the stars") in connection with astrological hopes.
desire.g: To want; to wish for earnestly.

desirous.e: From Middle English, from Old French desirrous, from desirrer + -ous.
desirous.g: Feeling desire; eagerly wishing; eager to obtain.

desolate.e: From Middle English desolaten (“to desolate”), from desolat(e) (“desolate”), from Latin dēsōlātus, perfect passive participle of dēsōlō (“to leave alone, make lonely, lay waste, desolate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) for more.

desolation.e: From Middle English desolacioun, from Middle French, Old French desolacion f, from Latin dēsōlātiō f.
desolation.g: The act of desolating or laying waste; destruction of inhabitants; depopulation.

despair.e: From Middle English dispeir, from Anglo-Norman despeir and Old French desperer (from Latin dēspērō, dēspērāre), or desesperer, from des- (“dis-”) + esperer (“hope”).
despair.g: To give up as beyond hope or expectation; to despair of.

despairing.e: From Middle English despeyringe, equivalent to despair + -ing.
despairing.g: Feeling, expressing, or caused by despair; hopeless.

desperate.e: From Middle English desperat(e) (“desperate”), borrowed from Latin dēspērātus, perfect passive participle of dēspērō (“to be without hope”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).
desperate.g: In dire need (of something); having a dire need or desire.

despicable.e: From Late Latin dēspicābilis, from Latin dēspicor, a variant of dēspiciō (“to despise”), from de (“down”) + speciō (“to look at, behold”). Equivalent to despise + -able.
despicable.g: Fit or deserving to be despised; contemptible; mean.

despise.e: From Middle English despisen, from Old French despis-, stem of despire, from Latin dēspicere (“to look down upon, despise, scorn”), from dē (“down”) + speciō (“to look at”).
despise.g: To regard with contempt or scorn.

despite.e: The preposition is derived from Middle English dispit, itself derived from the phrase in dispit of (in despite of).
From Middle English despite, dispite, dyspite, dyspyte, from Old French despitier.
despite.g: To vex; to annoy; to offend contemptuously.

despiteful.g: Full of despite; expressing malice or contemptuous hate.

despondent.e: From Latin dēspondēns, from the verb despondere (“to give up, to abandon”).
despondent.g: In low spirits from loss of hope or courage.

destine.e: From Middle English destinen, from Old French destiner.

destiny.e: From Middle English destine et al., from Old French destinee, from Latin dēstinō (English destine).
destiny.g: That to which any person or thing is destined; a predetermined or inevitable eventual state; a condition predestined by the Divine or by hum

destitute.e: From Middle English destitute, destitut, from Latin dēstitūtus.
From Middle English destituten, from the adjective (see above).
destitute.g: To impoverish; to strip of wealth, resources, etc.

destitution.e: From Old French destitution, from Latin dēstitūtiō (“abandoning”), from dēstituō.
destitution.g: The action of deserting or abandoning.

destroy.e: From Middle English destroyen, from Old French destruire, Vulgar Latin *destrugō, from Classical Latin dēstruō, from dē- (“un-, de-”) + struō (“to build”).
destroy.g: To damage beyond use or repair; to damage (something) to the point that it effectively ceases to exist.

destroyer.e: From Middle English destroyour, destroyere; By surface analysis, destroy + -er. Designating a warship, it is ellipsis of torpedo-boat destroyer, the longer term appearing at the end of the 19th century and the shorter form early in the 20th.

destruction.e: From Middle English destruccioun, from Old French destrucion, from Latin dēstrūctiō, dēstrūctiōnem.

destructive.e: From Middle English destructyve, from Middle French destructif, from Latin dēstrūctīvus, from past participle of dēstruere (“to tear down, destroy”) + -īvus.

detail.e: Borrowed from Middle French détail, from Old French detail, from detaillier, from de- + taillier (“to cut”).
detail.g: A part small enough to escape casual notice.

detain.g: To keep something from proceeding or coming to completion; to delay.

detect.e: From Latin detectus, perfect passive participle of detegere (“to uncover or disclose”), from de- + tegere (“to cover”); see tegument, tile, thatch. Sense "to work or solve cases as a detective" a back-formation from detective.
detect.g: To discover or notice, especially by careful search, examination, or probing.

deteriorate.e: Borrowed from Late Latin dēteriorātus, perfect passive participle of Late Latin dēteriorō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), further from Latin dēterior (“worse”).
deteriorate.g: To make worse; to make inferior in quality or value; to impair.

determinate.e: From Middle English determinate, determynat, determinat, from Latin dēterminātus, perfect passive participle of dēterminō (“to limit, set bounds”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more.
From Middle English determinaten, from determinat + -en, see Etymology 1 and -ate (verb-forming suffix) for more.
determinate.g: To bring to an end; to determine.

determination.e: From Middle English determinacion, determynacioun, from Old French determinacion, from Latin dēterminātiō. Morphologically determine + -ation.
determination.g: The act of determining, or the state of being determined.

determine.e: From Middle English determinen, from Old French determiner, French déterminer, from Latin determināre (“to bound, limit, prescribe, fix, determine”), from de + termināre (“to limit”), from terminus (“bound, limit, end”).
determine.g: To set the boundaries or limits of.

detest.e: From Middle French detester (French détester), from Latin dētestor (“to imprecate evil while calling the gods to witness", "denounce", "hate intensely”), from dē- + testor (“to testify, bear witness”), from testis (“a witness”); see test, testify.
detest.g: To dislike (someone or something) intensely; to loathe.

detestable.e: From Middle French détestable. By surface analysis, detest + -able.
detestable.g: Stimulating disgust or detestation; offensive; shocking.

detriment.e: From Old French detriement, from Latin detrimentum (“loss, damage, literally a rubbing off”), from dēterere (“to rub off, wear”), from dē- (“down, away”) + terere (“to rub”). Detriment is related to the word detritus, and built on similar foundations to the word impediment.

devastate.e: Borrowed from Latin dēvastātus, perfect passive participle of dēvastō (“to lay waste, devastate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)); from dē- (augmentative prefix) + vastō (“to destroy, lay waste”).
devastate.g: To ruin many or all things over a large area, such as most or all buildings of a city, or cities of a region, or trees of a forest.

devastation.g: The act of devastating, or the state of being devastated; a laying waste.

develop.e: Borrowed from French développer, from Middle French desveloper, from Old French desveloper, from des- + voloper, veloper, vloper (“to wrap, wrap up”) (compare Italian sviluppare, Old Italian alternative form goluppare (“to wrap”)) from Vulgar Latin *vloppō, *wloppō (“to wrap”) ultimately from Proto-Germanic *wrappaną, *wlappaną (“to wrap, roll up, turn.
develop.g: To discover, find out; to uncover.

deviate.e: From Late Latin dēviātus, perfect passive participle of dēviō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) for more.
deviate.g: To go off course from; to change course; to change plans.

deviate.e: From a substantivation of Late Latin dēviātus, see Etymology 1 and -ate (noun-forming suffix) for more.
deviate.g: A person with deviant behaviour; a deviant, degenerate or pervert.

device.e: From Middle English devis, devise, devyce, devys, devyse, from Old French devis and devise, from Latin dīvīsus, past participle of dīvidō (“to divide”).
device.g: Any piece of equipment made for a particular purpose, especially a mechanical or electrical one.

devil.e: From Middle English devil, devel, deovel, from Old English dēofol, from Proto-West Germanic *diubul, from Latin diabolus, ultimately from Ancient Greek διάβολος (diábolos, “false accuser, slanderer”), also as "Satan" (in Jewish/Christian usage, translating Biblical Hebrew שָׂטָן (śātān)).
devil.g: An evil creature, the objectification of a hostile and destructive force.

devilish.e: From Middle English develissh, develyssh, equivalent to devil + -ish.

devious.e: 1590s, "out of the common or direct way," from Latin devius (“out of the way, remote, off the main road”), from de via, from de (“off”) (see de-) + via (“way, road”). Originally in the Latin literal sense; the figurative sense of "deceitful" is first recorded 1630s.
devious.g: Cunning or deceiving, not straightforward or honest, not frank.

devise.e: From Middle English devisen, devysen, from Old French deviser, from Vulgar Latin devisō, from Latin dīvisō, frequentative of dīvidō.
devise.g: To use one’s intellect to plan or design (something).
The act of leaving real property in a will.

devoid.e: From obsolete Middle English verb devoiden, from Old French desvuidier (“to empty out”) (compare French dévider).

devote.e: Borrowed from Latin dēvōtus, past participle of Latin dēvoveō (“dedicate by a vow, sacrifice oneself, promise solemnly”).
devote.g: to give one's time, focus one's efforts, commit oneself, etc. entirely for, on, or to a certain matter; to consecrate.

devotion.e: From Old French devocion, from Latin dēvōtiō, from dēvōtum + -tio, from the supine of dēvoveō (“vow, devote”); equivalent to devote + -ion.
devotion.g: The act or state of devoting or being devoted; a feeling of being devoted (to something).

devour.e: From Middle English devouren, from Old French devorer (Modern French dévorer), from Latin dēvorō, from vorō.
devour.g: To eat quickly, greedily, hungrily, or ravenously.

devourer.e: From Middle English devourere; equivalent to devour + -er.

devout.e: From Middle English devout. From Middle English devout, devot, from Old French devot (French dévot), from Latin dēvōtus, perfect passive participle of dēvōveō.
devout.g: Devoted to religion or to religious feelings and duties; pious; extremely religious; godly.

dew.e: From Middle English dew, from Old English dēaw (“dew”), from Proto-West Germanic *dauw, from Proto-Germanic *dawwaz, *dawwą (“dew, moisture”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewh₂- (“smoke, haze”).
dew.g: Any moisture from the atmosphere condensed by cool bodies upon their surfaces.

dew.e: From Middle English dewe, dewen, from Old English *dēawian, from Proto-West Germanic *dauwēn, from Proto-Germanic *dawwāną.
dew.g: To wet with, or as if with, dew; to moisten.
